readerTitle: Your bakery needs 20% more. Where does it come from?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (동네 베이커리와 도매 거래처) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가격 인상은 하나의 숫자가 아니라 연속된 결정이다. 어디를 올릴지, 어떻게 알릴지, 무엇을 몰래 하지 않을지, 경쟁자에게 어떻게 반응할지를 각각 정해야 한다.
misconception: 가격을 20% 올려야 하면 모든 품목을 똑같이 20% 올리고 바로 적용하면 된다.

sources.text: 모든 수치와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시
이 유닛의 개념 레슨 (가격 인상, 공정성 인식, 슈링크플레이션, 가격 전쟁)을 종합한 시뮬레이션

factChecks.note: 크루아상 가격: $3.50 × 1.20 = $4.20 (정확히 20% 인상). 계산을 다시 확인하세요.
결과 카드: 평균 가격 +18%, 판매 수량 −4% → 매출 1.18 × 0.96 = 1.1328, 약 +13%. 모두 가상 수치입니다.
'원가 상승 때문이라고 설명하면 인상이 더 공정하게 받아들여진다'는 내용은 공정성 인식 연구(예: Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler 1986)의 일반적 결론에 기댄 것입니다. 카드에는 구체적 수치나 인용 없이 일반적으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Your bakery needs 20% more. Where does it come from?
body: You run a neighborhood bakery. You sell bread, pastries and coffee over the counter, and you supply loaves to 12 local delis and grocers.
Butter, flour and energy have all gone up. Your prices haven't moved in two years. Your accountant's verdict: to get back to last year's profit, prices need to rise **about 20%**.
Four decisions follow. Each one builds on the last.

image.label: Bakery counter with a chalkboard price list
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트 스타일. 동네 베이커리 카운터, 빵 바구니와 커피 머신, 뒤쪽 칠판 메뉴판. 주인이 계산기와 영수증 더미를 앞에 두고 고민하는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where does the 20% go?
body: Your regulars know the price of a plain loaf and a filter coffee by heart. Few could tell you what the lemon tart or the seeded rye costs.

image.label: Price board with some prices changed more than others
image.brief: 칠판 메뉴판 클로즈업. "Plain loaf", "Filter coffee" 옆에는 작은 화살표, "Lemon tart", "Seeded rye" 옆에는 큰 화살표. 품목마다 인상 폭이 다르다는 느낌.

options.feedback: Simple, but the biggest jumps land on the prices people remember. The plain loaf going up 20% is the thing regulars notice and talk about.

options.text: Raise the plain loaf and coffee a little, and the less-compared items more, so the average reaches about 20%
options.feedback: You get close to the money you need while protecting the prices customers use to judge you. The shop still feels fair.

options.text: Keep prices and switch to cheaper butter
options.feedback: It saves cost without a price tag change, but it changes the taste regulars come for. A quality drop is harder to undo than a price rise.

cards.title: Telling the 12 shops
body: Say you chose B. The counter prices are set. Now the wholesale side: delis and grocers that put your loaves on their shelves and set their own prices on top.
How do you bring them the new price?

options.text: Put the new price on next week's invoice
options.feedback: Fast, but a surprise on an invoice feels like a trick. The shops can't adjust their own shelf prices, and some will start calling other bakeries.

options.text: Call each one, give six weeks' notice and explain what your costs did
options.feedback: You give up six weeks of higher prices. In return, the shops can plan, and a rise tied to a real cost feels fair rather than greedy.

options.text: Leave wholesale prices alone so you don't lose accounts
options.feedback: You keep every shop, but wholesale quietly becomes the line that loses money. The rest of the bakery ends up paying for it.

cards.title: The croissant shortcut
body: Say you chose B. All 12 shops accepted, with some grumbling. Your baker has an idea for the $3.50 croissant: make it 15% smaller and leave the price alone. "Nobody weighs a croissant."

image.label: Two croissants, one noticeably smaller
image.brief: 나무 도마 위에 크루아상 두 개. 왼쪽은 크고 오른쪽은 조금 작음. 둘 다 "$3.50" 가격표. 작은 쪽에 물음표 하나.

options.feedback: No price shock today. But regulars who eat one every morning will notice, and a hidden cut feels worse than an honest rise.

options.text: Keep the size, raise it to $4.20, and show the new price clearly
options.feedback: Some customers will wince. But they know exactly what they're paying for, and the croissant still earns its place.

options.text: Keep it at $3.50 and add a mini croissant for $2.50
options.feedback: An open, smaller option is honest. But your best-seller still loses money on every sale, so the problem stays.

cards.title: The café down the street
body: Say you chose B. Two weeks in, a café down the street puts up a sign: "Coffee $2 all week." Three regulars mention it at your counter.

options.text: Match it: coffee at $2 this week
options.feedback: You win the week and lose the raise. Customers learn to wait for deals, and the café may cut again.

options.text: Hold your prices and say nothing
options.feedback: Holding is the right call, since their sale ends and your costs don't. But silence lets the comparison grow.

options.text: Hold your prices, and give regulars a stamp card: tenth coffee free
options.feedback: Your listed prices stay put, and loyal customers get a reason to stay that a one-week sale can't match.

cards.title: Say you chose C. Here's where you landed.
body: Fewer items sold also means less butter and flour bought, so profit is close to last year's level. The accountant's 20% was the target. The four decisions decided how much of it you actually kept.

breakdown.label: Average price
breakdown.detail: Plain loaf and coffee up a little, specialty items up more

breakdown.label: Items sold
breakdown.detail: A few customers left, most stayed

breakdown.label: Shops kept
breakdown.detail: Notice and a clear reason helped

cards.title: This path worked under certain conditions.
body: Your costs rose for every bakery in town, so rivals faced the same pressure. If only *your* costs had risen, customers would have had cheaper places to go, and a 20% rise could cost far more volume.
Explaining a rise by costs also creates a promise. If butter prices fall and yours don't, customers may remember the reason you gave.
cards.softwareNote: Software companies face the same four choices: which plans to raise, how much notice to give existing customers, whether to quietly remove features instead of raising the price, and whether to match a rival's discount.

cards.title: A price rise is four decisions, not one number.
list: **Decision 1 · Raising prices:** raise less where customers compare, more where they don't
**Decision 2 · Perceived fairness:** notice and a real reason make a rise feel fair
**Decision 3 · Shrinkflation:** an honest price beats a hidden cut
**Decision 4 · Price wars:** reward loyalty instead of matching a rival's sale
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list your five best-sellers. Mark the two prices your customers remember. Those are the ones to raise least.
